excerpt: Three hours, two directors, one last ride — Endgame sticks the landing even when it limps getting there.
markdown:
# Avengers: Endgame (2019) — Sample Draft

Look, I'll say it: I walked into this 181-minute closer braced for homework. Twenty-odd movies of homework. And for the first hour, my skepticism felt earned — it's slow, mournful, and structured like a support group with superpowers.

Then the time-heist kicks in, and I remembered why I put up with all of it.

Directors Anthony and Joe Russo were handed an impossible job — close out a decade-long saga, service two dozen egos, and still make it feel like a movie instead of a shareholder meeting. Mostly, they pull it off by letting the story breathe where it counts: Tony Stark tired and frayed, Steve Rogers out of time in every sense, Natasha Romanoff holding the whole thing together with duct tape and guilt.

## What works

The chemistry. Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans, Mark Ruffalo, Chris Hemsworth, and Scarlett Johansson have spent years building a shorthand, and it pays off here in small glances instead of big speeches. The film trusts you know these people, so a look between Tony and Steve carries more weight than another sky-beam fight.

The middle act is genuinely fun — a victory lap that replays old greatest hits with enough self-awareness to avoid feeling cheap. Hemsworth's washed-up Thor could have been a one-note joke; instead it's the film's saddest, funniest thread. And when the final battle finally arrives, it earns the noise. Every entrance lands because the movie made you wait for it.

## What doesn't

The pacing is lumpy, no way around it. The opening stretch wallows, the time-travel rules fold under any scrutiny, and a couple of character exits feel negotiated by contract rather than story. Ruffalo's arc in particular gets resolved with a shrug — smart guy now, moving on. Natasha fans have every right to feel shortchanged by how quickly the film moves past her.

And yes, at three hours and one minute, you'll feel the chair. The last twenty minutes try to be both a finale and a trailer for whatever's next, and those two goals fight each other.

## Verdict

Flawed, baggy, occasionally shameless — and still the only ending this saga could have gotten away with. It made me laugh, got me once (just once, don't tell anyone), and sent the two pillars of the franchise out with dignity.

**Rating: 8.5/10** — a messy, big-hearted goodbye that earns its tears.

excerpt: No one remembers Peter Parker — and honestly, forgetting the multiverse homework is the best thing to happen to this series.
markdown:
# Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) — Sample Draft

Thank god: a Spider-Man movie that fits in one neighborhood again.

After all the portals and cameos, this 145-minute reset from director Destin Daniel Cretton starts from a brutal, funny premise — Peter Parker (Tom Holland) is fighting crime full-time in a world that doesn't remember him, watching old friends move on without him. That's it. That's the hook. And it's the freshest the character has felt in years.

Holland plays Peter like a guy running on fumes and stubbornness, and it works. Zendaya's MJ gets less screen time than I'd like but makes every scene count, all sideways glances and unfinished sentences. The surprise MVPs of the lineup: Mark Ruffalo's Banner, who finally gets to be a weary mentor instead of a plot device, and Jon Bernthal's Punisher, who shows up like a brick through a window and recalibrates the stakes instantly.

## What works

Scale. The threat here is city-sized, not universe-sized, and the movie is better for it. Fights hurt. Web-swinging has weight again. Cretton shoots action cleanly — you can actually tell who's hitting whom, which in 2026 feels like a small miracle.

The "forgotten hero" angle gives Holland real pathos to play. He's not quipping through it; he's lonely, prideful, and screwing up in recognizably twenty-something ways. Jacob Batalon's Ned gets a bittersweet return beat that lands harder than expected precisely because the film doesn't oversell it.

## What doesn't

The villain problem isn't solved. The movie teases a powerful enemy no one can see, and "unseen" too often translates to "underwritten" — lots of menace, thin motivation. The middle sags when it has to explain how the new status quo fits the wider MCU, and one exposition dump feels piped in from a different movie.

The tone also wobbles in the last act, veering from scrappy street brawl to CGI soup for about ten minutes too long.

## Verdict

A lean, likable course correction. Not the best Spidey film, not close — but the first one in a while that feels about Peter Parker instead of about franchise management.

**Rating: 7.5/10** — smaller, sadder, swingier. More of this, please.

markdown:
# Avengers: Doomsday (2026) — Preview

No review yet — this one isn't out. Here's everything actually confirmed so far, without the fan-fiction.

## What we know

**Avengers: Doomsday** is dated **December 16, 2026**, currently listed as in post-production with a **165-minute** runtime. Direction comes from **Joe Russo and Anthony Russo**, returning to the franchise they closed out with Endgame.

The billed cast tells the story: **Robert Downey Jr.** is back, but credited as Victor von Doom / Doctor Doom — not Tony Stark. He's joined by **Chris Evans** (Steve Rogers), **Chris Hemsworth** (Thor), **Pedro Pascal** (Reed Richards / Mister Fantastic), and **Paul Rudd** (Scott Lang / Ant-Man). The official premise is deliberately thin: beloved heroes from three distinct universes are set on a deadly collision course against an existential threat unlike anything they've faced.

## Why it matters

This is Marvel's big swing back to event filmmaking. Bringing the Russos home signals the studio wants the Endgame magic again, and casting Downey as Doom — hero turned villain — is either a masterstroke or a panic button, depending on your generosity. Pascal's Reed Richards billing also confirms the Fantastic Four are central to whatever comes next, not a post-credits tease.

The "three universes" wording is doing heavy lifting. Expect the multiverse endgame to finally pick a lane — collision, not cameo parade.

## What to watch meanwhile

- **Avengers: Endgame (2019)** — the Russo playbook for juggling a dozen heroes without losing the emotional thread.
- **Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026)** — the street-level reset that shows the MCU can still do small stakes well.

excerpt: Pixar bottles teenage panic in 97 minutes — Maya Hawke's Anxiety runs the show and nearly runs away with the movie.
markdown:
# Inside Out 2 (2024) — Sample Draft

As someone who grades animated films on a curve (most of them are fine; few are honest), let me be precise about what director Kelsey Mann pulls off in these 97 minutes: a sequel that understands adolescence as a systems failure, not a mood swing.

Riley is a teenager now. Headquarters gets demolished overnight to make room for new Emotions, and Anxiety (Maya Hawke) arrives with a clipboard, a five-year plan, and absolutely no off switch. Joy (Amy Poehler), Sadness, Anger, Fear, and Disgust — a crew that had finally found equilibrium — suddenly look like middle management facing a hostile takeover.

## What works

Specificity. The film's model of anxiety isn't "feeling nervous"; it's over-planning, rehearsal, catastrophic what-if spirals. Hawke's performance is a marvel of pace — fast, bright, brittle — and the writing gives her behaviors, not just punchlines. Kensington Tallman's Riley grounds it: you believe this kid is performing okay-ness while unraveling inside.

Visually, it's Pixar at its most inventive since the first film. The new emotions' designs encode their functions — Anxiety's wide eyes, Envy's smallness, Ennui's magnificent horizontality — and the vault sequences find fresh gags in familiar architecture. Liza Lapira and Tony Hale slot into Disgust and Fear without missing a beat.

## What doesn't

The structure is conservative. If you saw the original, you know the beats: exile, road trip through the mind, race back before the core belief collapses. The new emotions beyond Anxiety get shortchanged — one could argue Envy and Embarrassment exist mostly for trailer moments. And the third-act resolution, while genuinely moving, arrives via a mechanism that feels more therapeutic pamphlet than narrative inevitability — true to life, maybe, but it sands down the climax into reassurance when the film had earned something thornier.

## Verdict

Smarter than it needed to be, kinder than it had to be, and funny in the margins — Ennui alone nearly justifies the ticket. It doesn't top the original's shock of recognition, but it deepens it — and Hawke gives one of the decade's best voice performances.

**Rating: 8/10** — the rare sequel that justifies itself psychologically, not just commercially.

movie.overview: Teenager Riley's mind headquarters is undergoing a sudden demolition to make room for something entirely unexpected: new Emotions! Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear and Disgust, who've long been running a successful operation by all accounts, aren't sure how to feel when Anxiety shows up. And it looks like she's not alone.
movie.title: Inside Out 2

excerpt: Bonnie gets a tablet, the toys get an existential crisis — a sweet, slight fifth outing that earns its goodbye-ish shrug.
markdown:
# Toy Story 5 (2026) — Sample Draft

Fifth movies have no business being this charming. I came in ready to file the franchise under "please let Woody rest" and left arguing with myself about screen time — never a bad sign.

The setup is painfully current: Bonnie gets a Lilypad tablet, gets obsessed, and suddenly Woody (Tom Hanks), Buzz (Tim Allen), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and the gang are competing with an algorithm for a kid's attention. Director Andrew Stanton — yes, that Andrew Stanton — runs with it for a tight 102 minutes, and the premise does real work instead of just delivering a moral about kids these days.

## What works

The ensemble still clicks. Hanks can do warmth in his sleep, but here Woody's steadiness reads as stubbornness, which is more interesting. Cusack's Jessie gets the film's best material — the toy who most needs to be needed — and Allen finds a lovely late-career softness in Buzz without sanding off the delusion. Newcomer Smarty Pants (Conan O'Brien, clearly having a blast) could have been a cheap gag and ends up the film's funniest idea about what "smart" toys actually optimize for.

The tablet rivalry avoids preachiness. The movie likes play in all forms; its complaint is with passivity, not technology. A couple of set pieces built around that idea are genuinely clever without needing to be loud.

## What doesn't

Let's be honest: the formula shows. Mission, separation, reunion, lesson — you've seen this route before, and the film doesn't hide it. Bonnie herself (Scarlett Spears) is more plot function than person this time, and the emotional high point lands a full tier below the franchise's best goodbyes. One farewell beat in particular feels engineered for trailers rather than earned by the story.

Visually polished, yes, but no longer surprising. Pixar's house style serves the characters fine; it just doesn't dazzle anymore.

## Verdict

Not essential, but genuinely sweet — the rare fifth entry that knows it's an epilogue and behaves like one.

**Rating: 7/10** — minor-key Toy Story, played with feeling by people who clearly love these toys.

excerpt: 140 minutes of pure visual anarchy with a bruised heart — the rare middle chapter that swings harder than the original.
markdown:
# Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023) — Sample Draft

I have seen a lot of animated movies try to look "comic-booky." This is the one that made me stop using the word as a compliment for anything else.

Miles Morales (Shameik Moore) reunites with Gwen Stacy (Hailee Steinfeld) and gets hurled across the Multiverse into the Spider Society — an army of Spider-People policing existence itself. When Miles and the Society split over how to handle a new threat, he ends up on his own against basically everyone. That 140-minute sprint, steered by directors Joaquim Dos Santos, Kemp Powers, and Justin K. Thompson, is the engine; the heart is two kids trying not to lose their families while saving every world at once.

## What works

Everything about the image. Each universe gets its own print logic, palette bleed, and frame rate — Gwen's world literally watercolors its mood. It's overwhelming on purpose and coherent by craft; I never once lost geography in the chaos, which is more than most live-action blockbusters manage.

The voice work is stacked. Moore keeps Miles grounded and teenage-specific even mid-multiverse meltdown. Steinfeld matches him beat for beat — her Gwen is all drums and deflection until she isn't. Brian Tyree Henry and Luna Lauren Vélez as Jeff and Rio Morales deliver the film's quiet gut punches, and Jake Johnson's Peter B. Parker remains the series' best joke-that-became-a-person.

## What doesn't

It's half a movie, and it knows it. The cliffhanger ending isn't a twist; it's a stop sign, and the last twenty minutes start to feel it — momentum traded for setup. The Society's bureaucracy stretches thin in places, with so many Spider-variants that most register as posters, not people. And at full tilt the sound mix occasionally buries dialogue under score and splatter.

Casual viewers should also know: this assumes you've seen the first one. No recap, no mercy.

## Verdict

A middle chapter with first-chapter energy. Messier than Into the Spider-Verse, more ambitious too — and when it sings, nothing else in the genre touches it.

**Rating: 9/10** — see it as big and loud as you can.
